body:
What is environmental remediation?

Environmental remediation means treating, removing, containing or reducing harmful contaminants in soil, water or other environmental media.

Contamination may arise from industrial discharge, agricultural chemicals, fuel leakage or inappropriate waste disposal. Different pollutants behave differently. Some are dissolved, some are attached to soil particles, and others are present as suspended matter.

Nanomaterials are useful in selected remediation methods because their surfaces can interact with pollutants and, in certain cases, support chemical reactions that transform them.

Three important remediation mechanisms

1. Adsorption

Adsorption is the attachment of a substance to a surface. A nanostructured adsorbent may capture selected contaminants, including certain dyes or metal ions.

For example, a suitable iron-oxide-based nanomaterial can interact with particular pollutants in water. After adsorption, the contaminant remains associated with the adsorbent unless it is subsequently separated, recovered or otherwise treated.

Adsorption must be distinguished from absorption, in which a substance enters the bulk of another material. The 2 processes are not identical.

2. Chemical transformation

Nanoscale zero-valent iron is commonly abbreviated nZVI. The term zero-valent refers to iron in its elemental oxidation state.

Under suitable conditions, nZVI can participate in reactions that transform certain contaminants, including selected chlorinated organic compounds. Such reactions may make the original pollutant less harmful, but the nature and safety of the products formed must also be considered.

When a treatment acts on a metal contaminant, it may change the metal's chemical form or mobility. It does not destroy the metal element itself.

3. Photocatalytic degradation

Some titanium dioxide materials act as photocatalysts. Under suitable illumination, they can promote reactions that break down selected organic contaminants.

Photocatalysis depends on light, catalyst properties and the surrounding medium. It cannot be assumed to work equally well on every pollutant or in every water source.

Using nanotechnology in soil and groundwater treatment

Soil and groundwater contamination can involve toxic metals, industrial solvents and other chemicals. Suitable nanomaterials may be investigated for capturing pollutants or changing their mobility and chemical form.

Effective remediation requires more than selecting an active material. Contaminants must be identified, the treatment must work under actual environmental conditions, and the possibility of new contamination must be controlled.

Remediation can also create environmental risks

A nanoparticle introduced for environmental treatment may itself move through soil or water. Some particles may remain suspended, while others may attach to soil or settle. This behaviour depends on their composition, surface properties and surrounding conditions.

Consequently, a remediation method should consider:

  • Whether the intended contaminant is actually removed or transformed.
  • Whether the treatment creates harmful reaction products.
  • Whether the nanomaterial can escape into the environment.
  • How used materials, residues and contaminated solids will be managed.

Capturing a pollutant is not the same as destroying it. Adsorption transfers a pollutant to a surface; photocatalysis may break down selected organic molecules; and chemical treatment may change the form or mobility of a contaminant.

Connection with conventional pollution control

Established processes such as filtration, sedimentation, biological treatment and pollution prevention remain important. Nanotechnology is one additional set of tools and is not necessarily the best method for every contamination problem.

Preventing a pollutant from entering the environment may sometimes be more reliable and economical than trying to remove it later.

Prelims focus

  • Remediation aims to remove, contain or reduce environmental contamination.
  • Adsorption means attachment to a surface.
  • nZVI stands for nanoscale zero-valent iron.
  • Suitable titanium dioxide materials can act as photocatalysts under appropriate illumination.
  • Used adsorbents and remediation residues may require further management.
  • Trap: Chemical treatment cannot destroy a metal element; it can change its form, mobility or location.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter Environmental Issues, sections on water pollution and waste treatment; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 164-168; U.S. National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, Applications of Nanotechnology, environmental remediation section, consulted 13 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Adsorption captures contaminants on a surface; nZVI changes selected contaminants; illuminated titanium dioxide helps break down selected organic pollutants.
pictures.caption: Adsorption, chemical transformation and photocatalysis treat pollutants through different mechanisms.

title: Nanotechnology for Pollution Control and Environmental Remediation

body:
What is nanotoxicology?

Nanotoxicology is the study of potentially harmful effects of nanomaterials on living organisms and biological systems.

At the nanoscale, properties such as particle size, surface area, shape and chemical reactivity can influence how a substance interacts with cells and tissues. As a result, safety information for a bulk material may not always be sufficient to assess a nanoscale form of the same substance.

However, the presence of nanoparticles does not automatically mean that a product is dangerous. Assessment must examine the specific substance and the circumstances of exposure.

Hazard, exposure and risk are different concepts

Hazard is the ability of a substance or situation to cause harm. Exposure is contact with that substance, including how much reaches a person and by which route. Risk concerns the likelihood and seriousness of harm under particular exposure conditions.

A hazardous nanoparticle tightly contained within a stable material may create a different exposure situation from the same nanoparticle dispersed as airborne powder. Containment may reduce exposure, although its effectiveness can change if the product is worn, damaged or disposed of.

Core distinction: A material's potential to cause harm is not identical to the likelihood of harm during a particular use. Risk assessment considers both hazardous properties and the exposure situation.

How can nanoparticles enter the human body?

Inhalation

Inhalation means breathing particles into the respiratory system. Airborne nanoparticles or particle-containing droplets may be inhaled during some manufacturing, handling, cleaning or disposal activities.

Some inhaled particles can deposit in the respiratory tract, including deep regions of the lungs. Their subsequent effects depend on the particles and the amount and duration of exposure. For workers handling manufactured nanomaterials, inhalation is a major concern addressed by occupational-safety guidance.

Ingestion

Ingestion means swallowing material. It may occur through contaminated food or water, or through unintentional hand-to-mouth transfer in a workplace.

After ingestion, a substance may pass through the digestive system, dissolve, interact with the intestinal surface or, in some cases, be absorbed. These outcomes are material-dependent.

Skin contact

Nanoparticles may contact the skin through products, spills or workplace handling. Skin penetration depends on the formulation, the condition of the skin and the properties of the material.

It is incorrect to assume that all nanoparticles penetrate intact skin merely because they are very small.

Intentional medical administration

Some nanomedicines are intentionally introduced into the body by an approved medical route. Their benefit-risk assessment differs from accidental exposure because the treatment is designed for a specific purpose and must be evaluated for safety and effectiveness.

What determines possible toxicity?

Nanomaterial toxicity cannot be predicted from size alone. Important factors include:

  • Chemical composition: Silver, carbon, titanium dioxide and lipid-based materials have different chemical and biological properties.
  • Particle size and shape: These influence movement, deposition and interaction with biological structures.
  • Surface characteristics: Charge, coatings and surface reactivity can affect biological interactions.
  • Solubility and dissolution: Some particles may release dissolved substances, including metal ions.
  • Dose and duration: The amount of material reaching an organism and the length or frequency of exposure influence the likelihood of harm.
  • Exposure route: Breathing a substance, swallowing it and receiving it as a medicine are not equivalent situations.

Possible biological effects

Studies of particular nanomaterials under particular exposure conditions have identified mechanisms such as oxidative stress, inflammation and cellular injury.

Oxidative stress occurs when reactive chemical species are produced or accumulate beyond a cell's ability to control them adequately. This can damage cellular components. Inflammation is a biological response that may help protect tissues but can also contribute to injury when excessive or prolonged.

Such effects should not be attributed to every nanomaterial. Experimental findings must be interpreted in relation to the material, exposure level, route and relevance to human conditions.

Why workers need special protection

Workers who manufacture, process or handle nanomaterials may encounter airborne particles before they are incorporated into finished products. Tasks involving loose powders or particle-containing aerosols can present different exposure opportunities from handling intact finished components.

The World Health Organization published guidelines on protecting workers from potential risks of manufactured nanomaterials on 2 February 2017. These guidelines emphasise reducing occupational exposure, especially inhalation exposure.

Prelims focus

  • Nanotoxicology studies harmful biological effects associated with nanomaterials.
  • Hazard, exposure and risk are related but different concepts.
  • Major exposure routes include inhalation, ingestion and skin contact.
  • Particle size, shape, chemistry, surface properties and dissolution can affect toxicity.
  • WHO issued worker-protection guidelines for manufactured nanomaterials in 2017.
  • Trap: A material's nanoscale size alone neither proves toxicity nor establishes safe use.

[Sources: World Health Organization, WHO Guidelines on Protecting Workers from Potential Risks of Manufactured Nanomaterials, 2 February 2017, executive summary and exposure-control recommendations; World Health Organization, Principles and Methods to Assess the Risk of Immunotoxicity Associated with Exposure to Nanomaterials, 12 April 2020, overview; U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, Nanotechnology Frequently Asked Questions, updated 3 March 2026; sources consulted 13 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Four nanomaterial exposure routes link circumstances to body contact; amount, route and duration affect risk, and exposure does not automatically cause illness.
pictures.caption: The main exposure routes depend on where and how nanoparticles are used.

pictures.alt: Hazard and exposure together determine risk; airborne powder and particles embedded in intact material create different exposure conditions.
pictures.caption: Health risk assessment combines hazardous properties with actual exposure conditions.

title: Nanotoxicology: Exposure Pathways and Human Health Risks

body:
What is environmental fate?

Environmental fate describes what happens to a substance after it enters the environment: where it moves, whether it changes form, and where it may eventually accumulate or be removed.

Engineered nanomaterials may enter the environment during manufacture, product use, washing, waste treatment or disposal. The extent and form of their release depend on the product and its management.

Movement through air, water and soil

Particles released into air may remain suspended for some time or become deposited on surfaces. Particles entering wastewater may remain dispersed, attach to other substances, or become incorporated into wastewater-treatment sludge.

Depending on how sludge is treated and used or disposed of, associated contaminants may be transferred to another environmental medium. Particles in soil may remain attached to soil components, move with water or undergo changes in chemical form.

Transformations that affect movement

Aggregation and agglomeration

Nanoparticles may cluster together. Aggregation generally refers to particles becoming strongly bound or fused, while agglomeration commonly refers to more loosely associated clusters.

Clustering can change how particles settle, move or interact with living organisms. A cluster can be larger than the individual nanoparticles composing it. Therefore, a nanomaterial does not necessarily remain as separate 1-100 nm particles after entering natural water.

Dissolution

Some nanomaterials can dissolve partly or completely. For certain metal-containing particles, dissolution may release metal ions. In such cases, environmental effects may be caused by the remaining particles, dissolved substances, or both.

Surface changes

Natural organic matter, dissolved salts and other environmental substances can interact with nanoparticle surfaces. These interactions may change particle stability, mobility or reactivity.

Consequently, a nanomaterial's behaviour in clean laboratory water may differ from its behaviour in a river, pond or agricultural soil.

Effects on plants, microorganisms and aquatic life

Under sufficiently high or otherwise harmful exposures, particular nanomaterials may affect soil microorganisms, plant growth, aquatic organisms or other living systems.

Potential effects include interference with normal cellular processes, changes in microbial activity or injury to sensitive organisms. The outcome depends on the material, the species, environmental conditions and exposure.

Soil microorganisms are important because they help decompose organic matter and recycle nutrients. Damage to these organisms can therefore have consequences beyond a single species.

Bioaccumulation and biomagnification

Two concepts must be distinguished:

  • Bioaccumulation: Build-up of a substance in an organism when uptake exceeds its elimination over time.
  • Biomagnification: Increase in the concentration of a substance at successive higher feeding levels in a food chain.

Some persistent conventional pollutants, including DDT and certain forms of mercury, are established examples used to explain biomagnification. Their behaviour depends on persistence and transfer through the food chain.

Nanoparticles may be taken up by certain organisms, but that observation alone does not prove that they biomagnify. The chemical form may change, particles may dissolve, and organisms may eliminate some of the material.

Biomagnification is not an automatic property of nanoparticles. Evidence of exposure or accumulation in one organism is insufficient to establish increasing concentration across successive trophic levels.

Why ecological assessment must be material-specific

A particle designed for antimicrobial action may be beneficial in a controlled setting but could affect helpful microorganisms if released into an unsuitable environment. Similarly, a nanomaterial used in remediation may create a secondary problem if it spreads beyond the intended treatment area.

Environmental safety therefore requires attention to the substance's properties, its release, transformation and exposure of non-target organisms.

Prelims focus

  • Environmental fate includes movement, transformation and final distribution of a substance.
  • Nanoparticles can cluster, dissolve or undergo surface changes after release.
  • Wastewater-treatment sludge can be a pathway through which associated substances move between environmental media.
  • Bioaccumulation occurs within an organism; biomagnification concerns successive food-chain levels.
  • DDT and mercury are established examples used to teach biomagnification.
  • Trap: Evidence that an organism has absorbed nanoparticles does not establish biomagnification.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Chapter Environmental Issues, section Water Pollution and the discussion of biomagnification; NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter Soil, printed pp. 96-98; World Health Organization, WHO Guidelines on Protecting Workers from Potential Risks of Manufactured Nanomaterials, 2017, sections on material properties and risk; U.S. National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, Applications of Nanotechnology, environmental applications section, consulted 13 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Released nanomaterials can move through air, wastewater, sludge, soil and water, changing by attachment, clustering, dissolution or surface changes.
pictures.caption: A released nanomaterial can move between environmental compartments.

pictures.alt: One organism accumulates pollutant when uptake exceeds elimination; DDT concentration increases up a food chain. Nanoparticle uptake alone does not prove this.
pictures.caption: Bioaccumulation concerns one organism; biomagnification concerns successive food-chain levels.

title: Environmental Fate of Nanoparticles and Ecological Risks
